name: Respiratory system
description: The airways and lungs: the nose, pharynx and larynx, the trachea and bronchi, the lobes and coverings of the lungs, how breathing works, gas exchange and its control, and common disorders. Picture questions show the lungs and airways, drawn see-through inside the rib cage, with one part highlighted to name.

source.name: Written for Study Buddy. Pictures rendered from BodyParts3D (© The Database Center for Life Science, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP).

questions.prompt: What are the two main jobs of the respiratory system?
answers: Bringing oxygen in and removing carbon dioxide
wrong: Making red blood cells and storing iron
questions.explanation: It also warms and filters the air, makes the sounds of speech and helps keep the blood's pH steady.

questions.prompt: Which part of the respiratory tract carries air but takes no part in gas exchange (the 'dead space')?
questions.explanation: From the nose to the terminal bronchioles. Only the alveoli and the tiny ducts leading to them are the respiratory zone. The dead space is about 150 mL.

questions.prompt: Which structures make up the upper respiratory tract?
answers: Nose, nasal cavity, pharynx and larynx
questions.explanation: The lower tract is the trachea, bronchi and lungs.

questions.prompt: What do the nasal passages do to the air we breathe in?
answers: Warm it, wet it and filter it
wrong: Change it from carbon dioxide to oxygen
questions.explanation: Hairs and sticky mucus catch dust, and a rich blood supply warms the air.

questions.prompt: What are the scroll-like bones in the side walls of the nasal cavity, which stir up the air flow, called?
questions.explanation: Superior, middle and inferior. The inferior concha is a separate bone.

questions.prompt: What are the air-filled spaces in the skull bones around the nose called?
questions.explanation: Frontal, maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid. They lighten the skull, warm the air and add resonance to the voice.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of the pharynx, from top to bottom?
questions.explanation: Only the nasopharynx carries air alone; the others carry both food and air.

questions.prompt: The auditory (Eustachian) tube joins the middle ear to which part of the throat?
questions.explanation: It evens out the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum. Yawning or swallowing opens it, which is why your ears 'pop'.

questions.prompt: Which flap of cartilage covers the entrance of the larynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: It keeps food and drink from entering the airway.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest cartilage of the larynx, forming the 'Adam's apple'?
questions.explanation: A shield shape, open at the back. It is larger in males because of testosterone at puberty.

questions.prompt: Which cartilage of the larynx forms a complete ring, at the bottom, joining it to the trachea?
questions.explanation: The only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. Cricoid pressure is used to close the oesophagus in emergency anaesthesia.

questions.prompt: Which structures in the larynx vibrate to make the voice?
questions.explanation: Air passing between them makes them vibrate. Tightening them raises the pitch.

questions.prompt: What is the opening between the vocal folds called?
questions.explanation: It narrows when we speak and opens wide in deep breathing.

questions.prompt: Which nerve to the vocal folds can be damaged in thyroid surgery, causing hoarseness?
questions.explanation: A branch of the vagus nerve. It loops under the aortic arch on the left and under the right subclavian artery on the right.

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The tube from the larynx to the carina, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: About how long is the adult trachea?
questions.explanation: It begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6) and ends at T4 or T5.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with the trachea in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: The cartilage rings of the trachea are C-shaped, with the gap at the back. Why?
answers: So the oesophagus can bulge into it when swallowing
So food can pass down the oesophagus behind it
wrong: So it can close more easily
questions.explanation: The gap is closed by a smooth muscle, the trachealis, which can narrow the airway, for example in a cough.

questions.prompt: What is the lining of the trachea?
answers: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells
questions.explanation: Mucus from the goblet cells traps dust; cilia sweep it up to the throat to be swallowed (the mucociliary escalator). Smoking paralyses the cilia.

questions.prompt: What is the ridge at the bottom of the trachea, where it divides into the two main bronchi, called?
questions.explanation: It is a very sensitive spot: touching it triggers a violent cough.

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The trachea divides at the carina into the right and left main bronchi, which keep branching inside the lungs.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which structures are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The tree of tubes carrying air into the lungs.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Why do swallowed objects usually end up in the right main bronchus rather than the left?
answers: It is wider, shorter and more vertical
It is wider and more in line with the trachea
wrong: It is closer to the oesophagus
The left one is blocked by the heart
questions.explanation: Which is also why a breathing tube pushed in too far goes into the right bronchus.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with the bronchi in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the airways, from the trachea down to the alveoli?
answers: Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
wrong: Trachea, bronchioles, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, alveoli
Trachea, lobar bronchi, main bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
Main bronchi, trachea, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
questions.explanation: About 23 divisions in all.

questions.prompt: Which airways have no cartilage and are controlled by smooth muscle that narrows in an asthma attack?
questions.explanation: Their lack of cartilage makes them easy to narrow.

questions.prompt: What happens in the airways during an asthma attack?
answers: The smooth muscle tightens and the lining swells and makes mucus
questions.explanation: A reliever inhaler, such as salbutamol, relaxes the smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: How many lobar bronchi are there in all?
questions.explanation: Three on the right and two on the left, one for each lobe.

questions.prompt: Which organs are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Two cone-shaped organs filling most of the chest, either side of the heart.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: How many lobes does each lung have?
answers: Three on the right, two on the left
wrong: Two on the right, three on the left
questions.explanation: The right lung has upper, middle and lower lobes; the left has only upper and lower, with a notch for the heart.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with both lungs in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
answers: Upper lobe of the right lung
Superior lobe of the right lung
wrong: Middle lobe of the right lung
Lower lobe of the right lung
Upper lobe of the left lung
questions.explanation: The top of the right lung, above the horizontal fissure. Note it is on the left of the picture, as we see the person from the front.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
answers: Middle lobe of the right lung
wrong: Upper lobe of the right lung
Lower lobe of the right lung
questions.explanation: Only the right lung has one. It lies between the horizontal and oblique fissures, mostly at the front.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
answers: Lower lobe of the right lung
Inferior lobe of the right lung
wrong: Middle lobe of the right lung
Upper lobe of the right lung
Lower lobe of the left lung
questions.explanation: The largest lobe of the right lung, below the oblique fissure. Seen here from behind, so the right lung is on the right.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways seen from behind, with one lobe in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
answers: Upper lobe of the left lung
Superior lobe of the left lung
wrong: Lower lobe of the left lung
Middle lobe of the right lung
Upper lobe of the right lung
questions.explanation: It includes the lingula and the cardiac notch where the heart sits, and is on the right of the picture.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
answers: Lower lobe of the left lung
Inferior lobe of the left lung
wrong: Upper lobe of the left lung
Lower lobe of the right lung
Middle lobe of the right lung
questions.explanation: Below the oblique fissure. Seen here from behind, so the left lung is on the left.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways seen from behind, with one lobe in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which organ is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Smaller than the right: it has two lobes and a cardiac notch, to leave room for the heart.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which organ is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Larger than the left, with three lobes, because the heart leans to the left.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which two fissures divide the right lung into its three lobes?
questions.explanation: The left lung has only the oblique fissure.

questions.prompt: What is the tongue-shaped projection of the left upper lobe, matching the right middle lobe, called?
What is the indentation on the front edge of the left lung called?
questions.explanation: It makes room for the heart.

questions.prompt: What is the area on the inner face of each lung where the bronchi, vessels and nerves enter and leave called?
questions.explanation: Together they form the root of the lung.

questions.prompt: The apex of each lung extends above which bone?
questions.explanation: It rises about 2.5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, so a stab wound at the base of the neck can puncture it.

questions.prompt: The base of each lung rests on which structure?
How many bronchopulmonary segments does each lung have?
questions.explanation: Each segment has its own segmental bronchus and artery, so a diseased segment can be removed on its own.

questions.prompt: What is the double-layered membrane around each lung called?
questions.explanation: The visceral pleura covers the lung and the parietal pleura lines the chest wall; between them lies a thin film of fluid.

questions.prompt: What holds the lung against the chest wall so that it expands when the chest does?
answers: The thin film of fluid between the pleural layers
Surface tension of the pleural fluid
questions.explanation: Like two wet glass plates that slide but don't come apart.

questions.prompt: What is air in the pleural cavity, which makes the lung collapse, called?
questions.explanation: The lung collapses because its elastic recoil is no longer opposed. A tube drain lets the air out.

questions.prompt: What is an excess of fluid in the pleural cavity called?
questions.explanation: From heart failure, infection or cancer, among others.

questions.prompt: What is inflammation of the pleura, causing sharp pain when breathing, called?
What is the central part of the chest, between the lungs, containing the heart, trachea and great vessels, called?
Which vessels supply the lung tissue itself with oxygen-rich blood?
questions.explanation: They come from the thoracic aorta. The pulmonary arteries carry blood to the alveoli to pick up oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which part is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. Seen here from the front and a little above.

figure.alt: The lungs and rib cage, with the diaphragm in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What does the diaphragm do when you breathe in?
answers: It contracts and flattens, moving down
questions.explanation: That enlarges the chest and the pressure inside falls below that of the air outside, so air flows in.

figure.alt: The lungs and airways inside the rib cage, with the diaphragm in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which muscles do most of the work in quiet breathing?
answers: The diaphragm and the external intercostals
questions.explanation: Quiet breathing out needs no muscle: the lungs and chest wall recoil like a stretched spring.

questions.prompt: Which muscles pull the ribs down and push the diaphragm up in forced breathing out?
answers: The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals

questions.prompt: Which neck muscles help to lift the ribs in hard breathing in?
questions.explanation: They are 'accessory muscles of inspiration'. Using them at rest is a sign of respiratory distress.

questions.prompt: Which gas law explains why air flows into the lungs as the chest expands?
questions.explanation: At a constant temperature, when the volume goes up, the pressure goes down.

questions.prompt: About how much air is breathed in with each quiet breath (tidal volume)?
questions.explanation: At about 12 breaths a minute, that is about 6 litres a minute.

questions.prompt: About how much air can a healthy adult breathe out after the deepest possible breath in (vital capacity)?
questions.explanation: Less in women and in smaller people. A spirometer measures it.

questions.prompt: What is the air that stays in the lungs after the strongest breath out called?
questions.explanation: About 1.2 litres. It stops the alveoli from collapsing completely.

questions.prompt: Where does gas exchange between the air and the blood take place?
questions.explanation: About 300 million tiny sacs, with a surface of about 70 square metres.

questions.prompt: How thick is the barrier between the air in the alveoli and the blood in the capillaries?
questions.explanation: The thin alveolar wall (type I cells) and capillary wall fuse, which makes the diffusion very fast.

questions.prompt: Which cells of the alveolar wall make surfactant?
questions.explanation: Surfactant cuts the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli so they don't collapse.

questions.prompt: What does surfactant do?
answers: Lowers the surface tension in the alveoli
questions.explanation: Premature babies lack it and get respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.prompt: Which cells in the alveoli engulf dust and bacteria?
How is most oxygen carried in the blood?
answers: Bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells
questions.explanation: About 98.5%; only 1.5% is dissolved in plasma.

questions.prompt: How is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
answers: As bicarbonate ions in the plasma
questions.explanation: About 70%. Red cells make it with carbonic anhydrase; the rest is on haemoglobin (about 23%) and dissolved (about 7%).

questions.prompt: Why is carbon monoxide poisonous?
answers: It binds to haemoglobin much more tightly than oxygen does
It blocks haemoglobin from carrying oxygen
questions.explanation: About 200 times more tightly. The skin may look cherry-red.

questions.prompt: What does a rise in carbon dioxide or acid do to the way haemoglobin holds oxygen (the Bohr effect)?
answers: It makes it release oxygen more readily
It lowers its affinity for oxygen
wrong: It makes it hold oxygen more tightly
questions.explanation: Working muscles make CO2 and acid, so they get more oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain sets the basic rhythm of breathing?
questions.explanation: With the pons helping to smooth it. The cortex can override it for a while (holding your breath).

questions.prompt: Which change in the blood is the strongest stimulus to breathe faster?
answers: A rise in carbon dioxide (or fall in pH)
questions.explanation: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to CO2 through the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid. Peripheral ones in the carotid and aortic bodies mainly respond to a fall in oxygen.

questions.prompt: Stretch receptors in the lungs stop breathing in when the lungs are very full. What is this reflex called?
Which nerve supplies the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: From C3, 4 and 5. A neck injury above that level stops breathing.

questions.prompt: What causes a hiccup?
answers: A sudden spasm of the diaphragm with the glottis closing
wrong: A spasm of the epiglottis alone
A spasm of the intercostal muscles

questions.prompt: What happens in a cough?
answers: A deep breath in, the glottis closes, then air is blown out explosively
A deep breath in and a forced breath out against a closed glottis
wrong: A slow breath out through the nose
Air is sucked in through the mouth only
The diaphragm relaxes and stays relaxed

questions.prompt: What is a low level of oxygen in the tissues called?
questions.explanation: A raised level of carbon dioxide in the blood is hypercapnia.

questions.prompt: What is a raised level of carbon dioxide in the blood called?
Breathing too fast and too deeply washes carbon dioxide out of the blood. What is the effect on blood pH?
questions.explanation: A person may feel dizzy and get tingling in the hands.

questions.prompt: What disease, mostly from smoking, combines chronic bronchitis and emphysema, with slowly worsening airflow limitation?
What is the breakdown of the alveolar walls, leaving fewer, larger air spaces, called?
questions.explanation: Gas exchange falls because the surface area does.

questions.prompt: What is infection of the lung tissue, which fills the alveoli with fluid and pus, called?
Which bacterium causes tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: It spreads in droplets and mainly infects the lungs.

questions.prompt: What is a blood clot lodged in a pulmonary artery called?
questions.explanation: Most clots come from the deep veins of the legs.

questions.prompt: In cystic fibrosis, a faulty chloride channel makes the airway mucus thick and sticky. Which chromosome carries the gene?
Which is the leading cause of lung cancer?
questions.explanation: About 85% of cases. Radon is the second most common cause.

questions.prompt: What instrument measures the volume of air a person can breathe in and out?
What does a pulse oximeter on the fingertip measure?
answers: The oxygen saturation of the blood
wrong: The carbon dioxide in the blood
questions.explanation: Normally 95% or more.

questions.prompt: About what percentage of the air we breathe in is oxygen?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up 78%. Breathed-out air still has about 16% oxygen, so expired-air resuscitation (mouth to mouth) works.

tests.name: Name the part
tests.why: Twelve pictures of the lungs and airways, each with one part in red to name.

tests.name: Chapter quiz
tests.why: Thirty questions from the whole chapter, marked at the end, like an end-of-unit test.

tests.name: Recall without choices
tests.why: Type each answer from memory, starting with the ones due for review. Small typos are forgiven.
